newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen says won't run for parliament.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen says won't run for parliament.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Wednesday he had decided against running in France's snap parliamentary election, but denied he was shying away for fear of defeat.
Le Pen's National Front party, which wants to send home three million immigrants, has no seats in parliament and opinion polls show it may win a handful at best in the snap poll on May 25-June 1.
"I will not present myself in the legislative elections," Le Pen, 68, told France Info radio, after days of dodging the question.

He accused President Jacques Chirac of staging a "hold-up", mainly to stifle corruption scandals, by calling the snap election almost 10 months early. He said Chirac should resign if his centre-right allies failed to win at least half the vote.

"This is a pseudo-referendum and (Chirac) should be judged on the number of votes received," Le Pen said. He added that he himself was not running because he would "be better occupied preparing for possible presidential elections".

Le Pen has sparked furious controversy in the past -- for example when he commented that the Nazi extermination of Jews in gas chambers was just a detail of history. He won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election.

Chirac has ruled out resigning if his centre-right allies lose the election, and the next presidential election is not due until 2002. Opinion polls show that his centre-right government allies are likely to retain power with a reduced majority.
In a later statement, Le Pen said he had also decided against running because he might fall foul of French laws barring politicians from holding too many elected offices.
Le Pen is a deputy of the European Parliament and a regional councillor in Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur region and said he aimed to stand for election as head of the region in 1998.

He denied he was scared his leadership would be weakened if he lost an election. The National Front has set a target of winning 20 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, but there are few constituencies where it has a chance.

Among the best-placed Front candidates is deputy leader Bruno Megret, whose wife is mayor of the southern town of Vitrolles, one of four National Front mayors. Megret has made clear he will not stand aside for Le Pen.

Le Pen, a former Foreign Legion parachutist, said his opponents "will say what they like. I don't think there are many of them in a position to give me lessons of courage, neither physical, military nor political".
He said Chirac wanted "to obtain a blank cheque" with the elections "to lead without any restraints the policy...that will bring submission to the Maastricht Treaty".

"This is a question of a risk of death for France and the French people," said Le Pen, a bitter opponent of closer European integration under the Maastricht blueprint, which he regards as sacrificing French independence.

"We think we are the only ones able to save the country from its risk of disappearing under Maastricht policies and from the evils battering it for 20 years -- unemployment, immigration, insecurity, taxes, falling birth rates, political and moral corruption," he said.
